newsitem.title: USA: Mass. Lt. Gov Cellucci wants surplus for tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Mass. Lt. Gov Cellucci wants surplus for tax cuts.

text.p: Massachusetts Lt. Gov Paul Cellucci said Tuesday he wanted to preserve the state's estimated $400 million surplus for tax cuts, debt repayment, and possibly, capital projects.

Cellucci told Reuters at the New England Governors' Conference: "The surest way to make sure the legislature doesn't spend it on expanding the operating budget is to give it back to the taxpayers. So these are the three things that we are trying to do."

The Lieutenant Governor, who is expected to take the helm once Gov. William Weld becomes U.S. ambassador to Mexico, declined to say how much money he would spend in each of the three categories, saying the Weld Administration still hoped the legislature would approve the seven tax cuts it proposed, which would reduce the funds available for other purposes.
The Weld Administration's tax cuts were projected to cost $82 million in the first year, but rise to $660 million in five years.

Asked how much debt might be repaid, Cellucci replied: "I don't want to put a number on it because our preference is tax cuts, and to the extent the legislature does not want to go along with the seven tax cuts we proposed, then these are other things we would consider."

Similarly, he declined to specify a minimum contribution for the state's Rainy Day Fund, a savings account that can be drawn upon if the state's economy turns down, though this was another area where the Weld Administration wants to increase funding for, saying how big a contribution was made also hinged on what was approved for the other categories.

Massachusetts has a $900 million cap on yearly capital expenditures, and using some of the 1997 fiscal surplus for one-time capital projects, like improving the state's environment and its seaports, would free up funds for other capital projects, he explained.

Cellucci predicted that the legislature and the Weld Administration would agree on a package of these various proposals. "I think we're going to see a combination. I think we're going to see some tax cuts, some money going into Rainy Day Fun and see some money spent on capital projects."

He did not take a stand on a dispute between the House and the Senate, which wants to use $134 million of the surplus for the last payment on fiscal recovery bonds sold by Massachusetts in the late 1980s to pay for operating expenditures. But he made it plain that the debt repayment he and Weld were considering would be in addition to the $134 million, noting that amount was due to be repaid in the 1998 fiscal year, which starts July 1.

Cellucci was wary of predicting that Massachusetts would enjoy another surplus in the new fiscal year, though he noted that a recent economic forecast, which showed the labor market continuing strong, was a hopeful sign. "If the unemployment rate keeps going down, I would expect that that means it's more likely we'll have (one), and who knows what it will be like next year or not, so I'm not projecting anything."
